articles.title_orig: German ministers vow tough response to Frankfurt riots and looting
articles.title_zh: German ministers vow tough response to Frankfurt riots and looting
articles.content_orig:
Cost-of-living protests that began in France have spread to Germany where demonstrations to coincide with Halloween took place on Saturday, with tens of thousands of people turning out across the country.
The new German youth-led movement dubbed “Gen Z has got this!” protested against the high cost of living, underfunded schools and universities, environmental concerns and a potential reintroduction of mandatory military service . Protests occurred in major cities including Berlin, Frankfurt, Cologne and Munich.
While the protest in the German capital appeared peaceful, water cannons and riot police were deployed in Cologne and Hamburg.
Police in Cologne said water cannons were used after some protesters set off fireworks during a march in the city center. “Our measures are directed against troublemakers and violent individuals – not against peaceful participants,” the police said in a statement.
In Hamburg, riot police responded after barriers were set on fire and emergency service workers were attacked. “There has been an increase in incidents of emergency personnel being pelted with pyrotechnics and construction (materials) … our riot police are taking immediate action against this,” the police said.
In Frankfurt, police said Molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency personnel and shop windows were smashed, prompting the closure of part of the Zeil shopping street. Officers arrested a suspect and seized two weapons after windows were broken at a gun shop.
Organizers of ‘Gen Z regelt’ planned the large day of action to coincide with Halloween, to maximize turnout and visibility. According to the organization, 120,000 people attended the protests across Germany on Saturday.
“We are young people who no longer want to watch decisions being made about our future without us,” the movement states on its website. It adds that the intention is to protest peacefully and organizers instruct participants to keep their faces visible, even in Halloween costumes.
Extra German police officers have been deployed nationwide in preparation for the protest, and the luxury shops lining Berlin’s upmarket Kurfürstendamm shopping street have boarded up their windows as a precautionary measure.
The German youth movement follows a broader wave of protests that have swept Europe, including significant unrest in France, which has been hit by rioting and looting and is now facing another weekend of rallies.
More nationwide protests from the Yellow Vests movement also took place in France on Saturday, in what has been billed as the third act of demonstrations, following earlier protests on October 17 and 24. Students and some unions are also expected to join.
French Interior Ministry said 320,000 people protested across the country on Saturday, with 70,000 turning up in Paris. That is a significantly smaller number than the 550,000 who demonstrated on October 17 and the 410,000 who showed up last week.
The ministry said that as of 6 p.m. local time, 296 people had been detained countrywide.
Warning of a “very high risk of public disorder,” France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez announced this week that demonstrations would only be authorized outside town centers, with 70,000 extra law enforcement officers deployed nationwide.
The protest were mostly peaceful, except for a few incidents. The Interior Ministry said in a statement that “radical elements at the tail end of the processions” in several cities. including Bordeaux, Toulouse, Rennes, Lille, Nantes, Marseille, and Lyon, “attempted to enter city centers with the intent to cause damage and engage in looting.”
The ministry said the police intervened and “thwarted” those attempts.
Jordan Bardella, the leader of France’s far-right National Rally party, said on X that “anyone who sends an ‘improvised incendiary device’ to law enforcement must be very severely punished,” adding that “perpetrators must rot in prison for very long years.”
Police in Rennes in Brittany in northwest France, said that while the main march planned for Saturday “proceeded calmly along the planned route,” several hundred violent individuals began attacking the police after the protest ended, throwing projectiles and setting off fires.
Violence has plagued the protests in recent weeks, with the ministry saying on Friday that as of October 29, at least 1,193 police officers had been injured since the start of the protests.
Halloween added a new complication to the protests, with Nuñez warning of separate calls for gatherings across France from 8 p.m. local time “by radical far-left groups and radicalized Yellow Vests.”
He said some messages invoked Halloween while calling for “revolution” and “insurrection,” describing them as incitements to serious public disorder and warning that the gatherings would be banned.
In recent days, the word “purge” has been circulating across social media platforms, a reference to the dystopian film franchise which depicts a world where all crime is legalized for a 12-hour period each year.
“At Halloween, the rules remain the same!” warned the Paris police on X, reminding people that concealing one’s face in public is punishable by a €150 ($170) fine, while carrying a weapon, even a fake one, can carry a sentence of up to three years in prison and a €45,000 ($50,398) fine.
The French protests began in late September, led by high school students demanding improvements to deteriorating school buildings, teacher shortages and a lack of resources, as well as changes to the university admissions system.
The protests then morphed into something bigger, with the Yellow Vests, which began as a movement against soaring fuel prices, among those taking to the streets.
The images of violence and looting from the October 17 protests are still haunting French officials. That day, more than 550,000 people took to the streets across France, according to the Interior Ministry, more than 3,000 shops were attacked or looted, with some destroyed and over 2,700 people were arrested.
Asked about the students injured during the protests, President Emmanuel Macron described the violence as a “collective failure.”
“I think no high school student started pushing for their demands expecting to suffer such terrible consequences. And I don’t know a single police officer who signed up to find themselves caught up in such terrible and violent moments either,” he told Youtuber Hugo Travers.
Saturday’s demonstration comes ahead of November 5, when all eyes will be on a nationwide strike and mobilization called by the inter-union coalition over rising living costs.
Alessandra Freitas contributed to this report.

Russia has suffered its deadliest month of the war in Ukraine since it began four years ago, according to figures released by Kyiv, as Ukrainian forces launched overnight strikes against a major Russian missile plant.
Ukrainian military officials have said throughout October, Moscow sustained 54,400 casualties. The figure surpasses the previous monthly high of 48,670 recorded in December 2024, with military planners warning that Russian frontline losses are now outweighing the Kremlin’s recruitment pipeline .
The claims coincide with deep-strike operations inside Russian territory overnight. Long-range Ukrainian drones targeted a facility manufacturing solid propellant and air-defence systems in the southern Rostov region, while more than 100 drones struck the industrial hub of Kstovo, east of Moscow, which processes five per cent of the country’s crude.
Russian forces launched retaliatory overnight barrages targeting Ukraine’s energy grid , firing 433 drones in a concentrated wave. The strikes severed power lines across several regions, leaving 280,000 households without electricity or heating.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky said the intensity of the Russian bombardments aimed to “take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors”, warning that critical civilian infrastructure remains under severe strain.
“Each month of the war is becoming increasingly costly for Russia's armed forces,” the Ukrainian general staff said in an update posted on social media.
While neither side publishes regular, verifiable accounts of their own casualties, current estimates place total Russian losses at more than 1.5 million personnel since the start of the conflict in 2022.
The casualty spike highlights Moscow's willingness to trade mass infantry losses for incremental territorial gains in the east.
Military analysts warn that exhausting manpower faster than regional recruitment bonuses can replace it leaves Russia vulnerable to strategic depletion, forcing greater reliance on foreign munitions and blunt mass destruction over tactical gains.
In the south, attention has turned to the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky , a Russian-occupied town on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River.
Situated as a strategic gateway to occupied southern territories and the approaches to Crimea, Oleshky's surrounding marshlands and river channels have become an entrenched amphibious battleground.
Civilians prepared on Saturday for the expiry of a rare six-day local truce – the most significant ceasefire between Kyiv and Moscow since the full-scale invasion began – which the White House said was brokered with the assistance of US first lady Melania Trump .
The brief window allowed hundreds of starved and exhausted Oleshky residents to evacuate via humanitarian convoys after supply routes collapsed under months of heavy drone and artillery fire.
Trapped for months in the crossfire of drone strikes and landmines, an estimated 2,000 residents had been pushed toward starvation before evacuees were bused out to both Ukrainian and Russian-controlled territories.
The acute plight of civilians trapped in the Dnipro basin prompted an intervention from the Vatican, with Pope Leo XIV raising the situation during his address and appealing for an immediate cessation of violence.
Local officials in nearby Kherson warned on Saturday that Russian forces had used the corridor’s quiet to reposition weapons and personnel, raising fears that heavy artillery shelling across the river would resume the moment the six-day truce expired on Sunday evening."
Ukrainian units have continued to strike Russian troop concentrations and logistics routes with precision drones and artillery.
The military escalation and relief efforts unfolded alongside high-level diplomatic activity in Ankara, where Zelensky held talks with Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdogan .
Discussions focused heavily on Black Sea shipping security , with both leaders warning that disrupted maritime corridors and looming grain shortages are threatening the world's most vulnerable populations.
Ankara is seeking to leverage its ties with both Nato and Moscow to broker upcoming trilateral talks that could restore safe commercial transit, facilitate prisoner exchanges, and establish a formal de-escalation framework.
Speaking after the meeting, president Zelensky insisted that any diplomatic resolution must respect Ukraine's territorial integrity, warning that formalising Moscow's territorial claims would invite future aggression.
Erdogan reiterated Turkey's support for Ukrainian sovereignty while offering to host negotiations, warning that a protracted war of attrition risks broader regional destabilisation.
The meeting followed comments from US secretary of state Marco Rubio , who welcome the idea of a ceasefire in the Black Sea.
“This is threatening the world for food security and some energy security as well,” Rubio said. “We'd like to achieve it. It doesn't solve the war, but at least it solves a unique aspect of it."
Rubio warned that the war cannot continue indefinitely as a battle of attrition and stressed that Western military assistance must be paired with realistic objectives. His remarks reflect growing pressure in Washington for an exit strategy .
By combining high-casualty frontline resistance and deep industrial strikes with localised humanitarian pacts and trilateral diplomacy, Kyiv and its partners are attempting to build maximum leverage before any formal negotiations begin.

articles.title_orig: You Might Be Neglecting The One Thing That Keeps Your PC Healthy
articles.title_zh: You Might Be Neglecting The One Thing That Keeps Your PC Healthy
articles.content_orig:
Updated: 17:01 EDT, 1 November 2026
The bone-weakening condition osteoporosis is often framed as a disease of old age, so I was horrified to be diagnosed with it at just 55. I felt booted into great-grandmama territory – weak and bleak, humbled and crumbling.
Here was the beginning of the end. I was travelling a road that I hadn't foreseen for myself, with falls and frailty ahead. Brittle bones are not sexy. It utterly changed how I saw myself – I felt weirdly ashamed.
But two years on, my health trajectory is transformed. I'm reversing my osteoporosis with training and nutrition alone, no medication necessary. And I'm stronger, inside and out, than I've ever been.
It sounds miraculous, and many doctors will tell you it isn't possible, but while there are caveats, I am proof that it can be done. Anyone can improve their bone health, no matter what age.
Before my diagnosis, I'd considered myself robust. In midlife I loved cold-water swimming, gracing the local lido four or five times a week all year round, even when the water was 5C (41F). I dabbled in yoga, regularly bothered about in the gym and did a slow 5K on the treadmill most weeks.
I also ate with deference to my gut microbiome – lots of vegetables, fruit, fibre, healthy fats, fish, chicken, yogurt, very little ultra-processed food. I didn't smoke, I barely drank – how dare this happen to me.
Yet it did. Thanks to a sharp drop in the bone-preserving hormone oestrogen, approximately half of post-menopausal women will suffer from osteoporosis and I was among them.
Turns out that the scattergun exercise I did was too light on lifting and bounding – insufficient to trigger osteogenesis, the body's natural bone-building response to impact and load.
It sounds miraculous, and many doctors will tell you it isn't possible, but while there are caveats, I am proof that osteoporosis can be reversed, writes Anna Maxted
Even seven years on HRT hadn't protected me. Since the age of 48, I'd taken an NHS-prescribed natural oestrogen called estradiol (plus progesterone) for perimenopausal symptoms – but while oestrogen boosts bone health and mineral density, it clearly couldn't manage the job alone.
I had no symptoms and would probably have continued tootling around in ignorance until the unhappy day, a decade or so hence, that I tripped over the cat and shattered a hip. As the NHS website notes, a fracture is often the first sign of osteoporosis, and if your skeleton becomes fragile enough, even a sneeze can snap a rib.
I was only spared this frailty-hastening fate courtesy of my cat thanks to a chance invitation from elite PT and founder of Evolution Longevity clubs, Matt Roberts. I'd interviewed him for work, and in the autumn of 2024 he invited me for a complimentary private bone scan at his clinic in Kensington, west London. At the time, aged 55, I didn't see it as a compliment – I was slightly offended.
But I accepted, a life-changing decision. Visiting sports therapist Paul Magee, of Profortis Bone Health, used the latest technology – an Echolight specialised ultrasound scan, which gives similar readings to a Dexa scan – to assess the bone mineral density in my hips and spine. He then told me: 'You are in the osteoporotic range.'
This was confirmed by several displeasing graphs, showing my BMD (bone mineral density) in the red.
BMD is measured by comparison with two norms – that of healthy young adults (T-score) and other adults your age (Z-score).
If you're over 40 and your T-score is less than -2.5 you have osteoporosis. The T-score in my left hip was -2.7 and my Z-score -1.7. In my spine, my T-score was also -2.7, and my Z-score -1.6.
Wow. I didn't even have osteopenia – lower than normal bone density, a precursor and warning sign for bone loss – I had the full-blown disease.
Anna with her trainer Matt Robert, who invited her for a complimentary private bone scan at his clinic in Kensington
Anna's bone-building mission at Evolution consisted of just three hour-long sessions of training a week
I was aghast. I felt embarrassed because I knew that strength-training was advised for women my age – we never stop hearing about it. I'd just chosen not to listen.
I slunk home despondent, and gloomily perused the NHS website which warned about avoiding 'a fall' and stated 'osteoporosis can be treated with bone strengthening medicines'. Were drugs really my only option?
An older family friend with the condition had been prescribed bisphosphonates – which slow bone breakdown – but they were so tough on her gut, causing stomach pain and difficulty swallowing, that she had temporarily come off them.
My husband insisted that I demand a second opinion on the NHS. As if. The Royal Osteoporosis Society notes that there's no national osteoporosis screening programme for anyone at risk, and that NHS fracture liaison services – if your local trust even has one – only diagnose osteoporosis in adults over 50 after you've had a low-impact fracture. Well, that's shutting the stable door after the horse has bolted and broken a leg.
Meanwhile, I felt like rolling myself in bubble-wrap and not moving. I'd been fast-forwarded to infirmity – and was quietly panicking. But Matt Roberts' evidence-based belief was that he and his A-team of trainers, nutritionists and physiotherapists could reverse my osteoporosis.
In 2017 there was a randomised controlled trial in Australia, the LIFTMOR trial, in which postmenopausal women, average age 65, all with a T-score of -1 or less (that is, they had osteopenia or osteoporosis) did 30 minutes of supervised progressive strength-training twice a week. After eight months, their hip and lumbar spine bone density had increased in a 'clinically significant' way.
Jon Roberts, technical director at Evolution (and Matt's brother) says: 'The LIFTMOR trial showed a fairly consistent – 0.3 to 3 per cent – increase in bone density. It provided the first categorical information that strength-training works – and it works better than anything else - in building bone.'
This is because – to quote an article published in January on osteoporosis in Harvard Medical School's journal Harvard Health – 'activities that put stress on bones can nudge bone-forming cells into action. That stress comes from the tugging and pushing on bone that occur during strength-training.'
Then I interviewed an NHS osteoporosis specialist. The doctor scoffed 'You won't be lifting weights at 80', adding that trying to increase my bone density this way would be like turning on a tap to fill a sink with an open plughole.
One can feel crushed when faced with such a scathing clinician – even if, bizarrely, they've ignored the latest research. Of course, medication is sometimes necessary. And of course, weight-lifting is not suitable or safe for everyone. But I strongly feel that it's a disservice to tell people that lifestyle changes are pointless, just take the pills.
Because guess what. Last month – two years into Roberts' regime of targeted strength and impact training – I had another scan. The bone mineral density in my left hip has increased by 11.4 per cent. As for my spine, there's been a 4.4 per cent net gain in bone density in two years.
How did I achieve this? My bone-building mission at Evolution consisted of just three hour-long sessions of training a week. But it was specifically designed to make my lazy bones realise they had to toughen up for the work I now required of them.
Crucially, 'we started with the foundations'. My brilliant, diligent PT Ollie Cascarina initially focused on improving my quality of movement – building strength in my glutes and core. This involved bodyweight exercises such as glute bridges, planks, squats and lunges. I also did weighted squats, weighted lunges, and endless pulling and pushing weights on various ghastly machines.

articles.title_orig: Inside the leaderless movement set to govern Serbia
articles.title_zh: Inside the leaderless movement set to govern Serbia
articles.content_orig:
Serbia's victorious student-led movement has called for top figures in the police, intelligence and judiciary to stand down, days after ousting ex-president Aleksandar Vučić's party from power.
Standing in Pioneers' Park opposite parliament, newly elected MPs on the Student List demanded the immediate dismissal of all police officers who had broken the law, singling out the heads of the police, the BIA security agency and anti-terror unit.
It is not often a European country votes to fully reset its political system overnight, and Serbians have voted to hand the task to a group of novice politicians, made up of intellectuals, professors, artists, athletes and as many as 12 medical doctors and surgeons.
But the handover of power will take weeks, and the students' movement is concerned that evidence of possible wrongdoing could be destroyed in that time.
Just a few days ago, the park they were standing in on Thursday was a tent camp, filled with Vučić loyalists outside his office.
Within hours of him admitting defeat on Sunday night, the camp was dismantled, and a team of volunteers moved in on Monday morning to clean up the mess.
"This is just the first wave of spring cleaning, the new ones are coming now - we are very excited but ready to do it too," said Marija Milovanović, 25, as she scrubbed a park bench.
The student movement emerged from protests following the fatal collapse of a railway station canopy that killed 16 people in November 2024, in Serbia's second largest town Novi Sad.
Their desire was to bring those responsible to justice, and investigate widespread corruption claims blamed for one of the most tragic events in Serbia's modern history.
They have made some bold promises.
Under their Student Plan, they promise to "halt the plunder, return stolen goods to the state budget, and invest directly in education and the economy".
The purge of Vučić loyalists has already begun at Serbia's state broadcaster RTS, where director Manja Grčić has stepped down.
Newly elected MP Mirjana Nikolić said Serbian citizens had the right to truthful information and RTS had served the interests of the government for years.
The new MPs have also set their sights on replacing the head of Telekom Srbija, Vladimir Lučić.
Vučić loyalist Ana Brnabić, who is currently Serbia's acting president, has accused her opponents of choosing "revolutionary justice, not rule of law," and of aiming to shut down "all of the media they dislike".
But one of the next government's best-known MPs, Dejan Šoškić, argues that key reforms need to be in place fast.
"In the first six months, I would like to see the media scene liberated, fighting against corruption on the way, the institutions operating as prescribed by laws and a lustration law introduced," said Šoškić, an economist who served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012.
By lustration, he means banning from public office members of the Vučić government or party apparatus who are found to have violated the rights of Serbians.
That kind of purge will take time, as all of Serbia's main pillars of authority have been held by Vučić and his party for so long, warns Strahinja Subotić of Belgrade-based European Policy Centre.
Ultimately, he believes the new administration will have to "build bridges to the segments that have been operating well in the past".
All 141 successful candidates were chosen by students from universities across Serbia through a lengthy, secretive and carefully crafted process, and tasked with implementing the movement's plan for a complete rebuild of the country.
That political agenda took months for a highly diverse group of students to agree to. Now it is up to the equally disparate team of successful candidates to put the plan into practice, rather than the students themselves.
Another prominent figure on the Student List, is Radomir Saičić, a professor of organic chemistry at the University of Belgrade.
"While the practical mechanisms will be developed on the go, the new MPs will stick to the students' 1200-page long and detailed plan," he told the BBC.
"Parliament is making decisions, but since this change was led by students' efforts, we would highly value their opinion and work closely with them," he promised.
Not only are they newcomers to politics, but Serbia's election winners have no obvious leader and are faced with a series of complex challenges, including taking on the country's highly complex balancing act on the international stage.
Serbia is both a candidate to join the European Union and maintains close relations with Russia. Its bid to join the bloc has long been on the back-burner, while its Western Balkan neighbours press ahead.
The EU was quick to welcome the Student List victory and has promised to back their push for reforms to the rule of law, media freedom and fight against corruption.
But EU integration occupies a strikingly minor place in the students' election manifesto, which describes the bloc merely as Serbia's "most important economic partner".
For years, Belgrade has balanced its foreign policy between the EU and its eastern partners, Russia and China. Belgrade has managed to stand out in Europe by not imposing sanctions on Moscow since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In return, Serbia has been rewarded with preferential gas prices that have helped maintain domestic stability, and Vladimir Putin publicly endorsed Vučić's bid to remain in power.
That does not mean that the students have any plans to change course, and changing Serbia's foreign policy may not be high on their list.
"Serbia had it own experience with sanctions in the 1990s and we know that they mostly harm ordinary people and do not affect policies of a state," said Dejan Šoškić, referring to UN sanctions imposed during the wars in former Yugoslavia.
The new government's initial focus will most likely be on domestic reform, and the clock is already ticking before the next election campaign, with presidential elections due to take place in December.
Aleksandar Vučić is legally barred from running for a third term as president, but he has promised that his defeated Serbian Progressive Party will fight back: "We will beat them much faster than they can even imagine."

President Donald Trump had a tense exchange with a reporter at his Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago on Saturday night.
The president briefly took questions in the ballroom of his Palm Beach resort , flanked by Secret Service agents and surrounded by partygoers in top hats, feathered headdresses, wings and sparkles.
“Do you expect to go back to war with Iran this week,” a reporter asked the president, who said he came dressed as “Donald Trump.”
“Why would you ask such a stupid question?” Trump snapped back, indicating that the reporter was from The New York Times .
“Let’s say I did, would I tell you? Let's say I didn't, would I tell you?” Trump said, throwing his hands up in the air. “I can’t tell you that…It’s not a question for The New York Times .”
The president has long had a combative relationship with the press , launching personal attacks on reporters, seeking to bar them from the White House and filing multimillion-dollar lawsuits against media outlets. Last month, he berated The Independent ’s Andrew Feinberg in the Oval Office, calling him a “sick person” who “better be careful.”
Speculation has mounted for weeks that Trump, 80, will launch a new offensive against Iran following the midterm elections on Tuesday, which will determine which party controls the House and the Senate.
U.S. officials warned several Gulf allies to prepare for a short, intense military campaign after Election Day as Trump weighs renewed strikes on Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, two diplomats briefed on the matter told The Associated Press this week.
The president also reportedly met with top military leaders on Thursday, including Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of U.S. Central Command.
“We may do another little Epic Fury,” Trump said at a rally on October 23, referring to the U.S.-Israeli bombing campaign this past spring. “Or they’ll agree.”
Eight months into the war, large-scale attacks have largely paused, but the fragile lull has left no clear end to the conflict in sight.
The war has led to the deaths of at least 18 U.S. service members and wounded hundreds more. It has also reportedly cost the U.S. military at least $47 billion and dramatically driven up fuel prices . Multiple polls indicate the war is broadly unpopular.

articles.title_orig: Burnham ‘open’ to UK slavery apology, but not reparations: Why now?
articles.title_zh: Burnham ‘open’ to UK slavery apology, but not reparations: Why now?
articles.content_orig:
King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade, during the final leg of his Caribbean tour in Antigua, Buckingham Palace has said.
The King will address Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday in a speech which will touch on the issue.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier he was "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery - a change in the government's stance.
It is understood the Palace was told in advance of Burnham's comments in an opinion piece on Friday night, and the King has not made any changes to his speech in light of them.
The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.
Burnham has previously stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.
In an address to the nation to mark Antigua and Barbuda's independence day, Prime Minister Gaston Browne said the history of slavery was painful and "its consequences have not disappeared with the passage of time".
He said the country's pursuit of reparatory justice deserved "seriousness, sensitivity and sustained international engagement".
Browne went on to say his government was having these conversations in bilateral discussions with the UK and other Commonwealth countries at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described "endless talk about apologies" as a "distraction" from solving current problems.
She told BBC Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "The transatlantic slave trade happened centuries ago. It is time for the Commonwealth to start looking forwards, not endlessly backwards."
The King will make his speech at the CHOGM.
He "will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit", a Palace spokesperson said.
"You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow, and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at CHOGM and beyond."
When asked about the King's reaction to the prime minister's comments, the spokesperson said it would "not be appropriate" for the King to address matters of policy relating to "the UK government's position".
The Caribbean tour has again thrust King Charles into the difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.
On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech where he spoke of the "suffering of the past".
In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.
Buckingham Palace said it was a moment for the King to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance. His engagements have also covered the environment, opportunities for young people and trade relationships with the UK.
Royal sources have stressed that the decisions around making an apology are a matter for government, not the Palace.
"His Majesty is well practised on the diplomatic tightrope," a Royal aide said. "He is up for challenging visits with complex issues and relationships in play. He sees it as his role to 'bat for Britain', the Realms and wider Commonwealth."
In a piece for the Guardian published on Friday night, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade as a "brutal and barbaric violation" , and that Britain "must face up to the past".
His separate pledge in his article to strengthen the work of the Commonwealth as an organisation will be welcomed by King Charles, who views the collection of 56 countries as a powerful vehicle for change.
The King will be giving the opening speech at CHOGM, which gathers leaders from those 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth.
Each biennial meeting has a theme and this year's is officially called Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.
Queen Camilla is with the King in Antigua and, as the couple attended a church service on Sunday morning ahead of joining celebrations to mark Independence Day on the island, there was a reminder of what the intended focus of the week will be.
Bishop of North Eastern Caribbean and Aruba,  Ernest Flemming, told the congregation the "prosperity" of the Commonwealth must be a "shared prosperity".
"True partnership requires mutual respect, it requires listening, it requires fairness."
A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: "Institutions are under strain across the globe. The Commonwealth has scale and breadth, but is also small enough for leaders to know each other and co-operate together."
The King, they said, "contributes ideas and encouragement on a wide range of issues, delivering practical results which help improve the lives of millions".
It has been a difficult few months for the King, with developments surrounding his brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor , and the publication of a book by his former brother-in-law, Earl Spencer.
In addition, his son the Duke of Sussex made a surprise move back to the UK with his wife Meghan and their two children in August.
Asked if the King was confident that his approach to family matters had been the right one in terms of public attitudes towards the institution, the response was concise. "Yes," a senior aide told the BBC. "That is why he takes the actions he does - and has done."
On the serious allegations that have emerged about Meghan's father , Thomas Markle, the Palace did not want to get involved publicly: "We wouldn't comment on private family matters."
The King is also still being treated for cancer. He was diagnosed in early 2024 and the Palace says he remains on a "positive trajectory".
In hot and humid conditions, he will soon celebrate his 78th birthday and will have carried out about 36 engagements by the end of this nine-day tour of the Caribbean.

articles.title_orig: Modded RTX 2080 Ti With 22 GB Memory Delivers Up To 73% Boost At 4K Compared To 11 GB Variant, Benchmarks Reveal
articles.title_zh: Modded RTX 2080 Ti With 22 GB Memory Delivers Up To 73% Boost At 4K Compared To 11 GB Variant, Benchmarks Reveal
articles.content_orig:
As expected, the GPU with twice the VRAM performed much better in certain scenarios, but not every game saw similar improvements.
German publication PC Games Hardware recently bought a modded GeForce RTX 2080 Ti from Alibaba, an eight-year-old GPU from the Turing family and the first flagship RTX offering from NVIDIA. The original card comes with 11 GB of GDDR6 VRAM, but by replacing the 1 GB modules with 2 GB Samsung GDDR6 chips, the modded card got a good 22 GB of VRAM capacity.
Such a memory size is generally more than sufficient for modern gaming, but back then, 11 GB was all you needed. Fast-forward to 2026, and games have started gobbling up a huge amount of VRAM, making many 8 GB modern offerings obsolete if you want consistent and smoother performance in modern triple-A titles. The tests by PC Games Hardware revealed how much of a difference it can make going from 11 GB to 22 GB, and here are the results.
When tested at QHD or 1440p resolution with DLSS set to Quality, the RTX 2080 Ti 22 GB offered similar performance to the 11 GB variant, but there were some exceptions. Flight Simulator 2024 saw a good 29% improvement, including better lows. Then we have Spider-Man 2 , which favored the 22 GB variant heavily, delivering nearly 22% higher FPS on average. Other titles such as Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, Cyberpunk 2077, Gears of War: E-Day , etc., didn't see any noticeable boost.
However, switching to 4K immediately showed the importance of higher VRAM capacity in modern titles. At 4K with DLSS set to Performance and FSR Frame Generation enabled, Flight Simulator 2024 showed nearly 73% higher performance, while Spider-Man 2 crossed the 60 FPS mark by achieving a solid 64% improvement. Even games that previously didn't record any noticeable difference were now running at a much higher FPS.
The frametimes charts clearly showed how much of a difference adding twice the VRAM capacity made to gaming, but gaming alone didn't benefit from increased memory. Even the AI workloads got executed way quicker than on the 11 GB variant.

articles.title_zh: At 75, the IRS Will Set the Withdrawal Amount on a $900,000 401(k). Affluent Investors Over 60 Are Making Sure It's Empty by Then - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
The IRS gets to decide how much comes out of your 401(k) at 75, and the tax cascade that follows can push your effective marginal rate past 40 percent. There is a narrow window before that clock runs out, and…
The Full Benefits Desk desk. Editor: Gerelyn Terzo .
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Picture a 62-year-old with $900,000 in a traditional 401(k) and a retirement date coming up soon. He doesn’t want the IRS setting his withdrawals later. If he leaves the account alone, the IRS starts making that call at 75.
Many people are working through the same problem. On Reddit, a 54-year-old with $720,000 in a 401(k) was told, “You’ll probably do a more substantial amount after 65 once you’re on Medicare.” That timing can be expensive.
Under current law, the required minimum distribution (RMD) starting age is 75 for anyone who turns 74 after December 31, 2032. Our 62-year-old was born in 1964, so that rule covers him. If he skips a required withdrawal, he can face a 25% excise tax, falling to 10% if corrected in time.
Roth IRAs get different treatment. The original owner never has to take required minimum distributions while alive. Every dollar that moves to a Roth before 75 is a dollar the IRS can’t force out later.
Assume 5% annual returns and 13 years until age 75. To empty the account by then, he needs to take out about $91,250 at the start of each year.
If he leaves it untouched, the same $900,000 grows to roughly $1.7 million by 75.
The IRS Uniform Lifetime Table divisor at that age is 24.6, so his first RMD comes to about $69,000.
By 85 the divisor drops to 16.0, which increases the required share of the balance from about 4% to over 6% a year.
Say he files jointly and the withdrawal is the couple’s only taxable income early in retirement. The 2026 standard deduction of $32,200 leaves $59,050 of taxable income.
All of it lands in the 10% and 12% brackets, and the 12% bracket runs up to $100,800.
The federal bill is about $6,590, an effective rate near 7%. Whatever part he doesn’t need to live on can instead move directly into a Roth IRA through a taxable rollover. Emptying the pretax account and spending the money are two separate decisions. That converted money can keep growing, with qualified withdrawals tax-free.
Now picture the untouched account at 75, with RMDs stacked on top of Social Security. On a joint return, benefits start becoming taxable once combined income passes $32,000, and the second threshold is $44,000. Up to 85% of benefits can end up taxable.
In that phase-in range, each extra RMD dollar taxed at 22% draws 85 cents of benefits into taxable income along with it. That works out to an effective marginal rate of about 41%.
After the year one spouse dies, the survivor generally files single. Under 2026 rules, the first Medicare surcharge threshold falls from $218,000 to $109,000.
Medicare’s income-related monthly adjustment amount (IRMAA) generally uses income from two years earlier. A conversion at 62 ordinarily won’t affect his Medicare premiums at 65. From 63 on, conversions can affect future premiums. That makes 62 an attractive window, although health insurance costs before Medicare matter too.
Under 2026 rules, a $91,250 conversion alone sits below the joint threshold of $218,000. Add a large capital gain on top and the couple could cross it.
The first level adds $81.20 a month per person to the standard $202.90 Part B premium , plus $14.50 for Part D.
For a married couple who can convert at around 7% now instead of facing a possible 41% marginal rate later, emptying the 401(k) on their own schedule comes out ahead.

A veteran financial journalist, she covers agri-finance for outlets like Global AgInvesting and the broader stock market and personal finance for 24/7 Wall Street. She began at CNBC and later helped launch Fox Business in New York. Gerelyn currently resides in Woodland Park, Colorado and dabbles in nature photography as a hobby.
The IRS hands a 72-year-old with a large traditional IRA one last window to shape their future tax bills before the rules lock in, and most retirees waste it by waiting until the deadline…
Leaving a seven-figure 401(k) untouched between retirement and age 73 sets up a tax collision most retirees never see coming until the IRS hands them a forced withdrawal they never asked for.

articles.title_orig: Israel election: When will government be formed, who will lead it?
articles.title_zh: Israel election: When will government be formed, who will lead it?
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his coalition’s parliamentary majority following legislative elections on October 27.
But a bloc of Jewish parties opposing Netanyahu also failed to win a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, leaving Israel without a clear path to a new government.
What’s ahead is likely weeks of political wrangling as Israel’s disparate factions weigh possible governing arrangements, including a unity government bringing rival factions together or a minority government reliant on outside support. If they fail to reach an agreement, Israel could head back to the polls.
Here’s what you should know:
The pro-Netanyahu coalition won 53 seats:
A bloc of Jewish parties opposing Netanyahu won 48 seats:
Arab-led parties won 19 seats:
That leaves all existing blocs short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, meaning some parties would have to realign or join forces across bloc lines to form a new government.
Israel’s election results must be officially certified and presented to President Isaac Herzog by November 4 .
The new Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on November 10 .
Herzog must task one incoming Knesset member with forming a new government by November 11 . He is expected to make his decision with input from party leaders, selecting the candidate he believes has the best chance of building a coalition.
The candidate commissioned by Herzog has 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible extension of 14 days .
He has not said yet, but the most likely candidates are Netanyahu or former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar party received the most votes in the opposition bloc.
According to Israel’s Yedioth Ahronoth media, Eisenkot may have an edge over Netanyahu as some Arab-led parties consider endorsing him in a bid to oust Netanyahu.
Herzog, for his part, has urged Israeli politicians to move away from rigid partisan stances and look for “creative solutions” that will lead to a new government and avoid a second round of elections.
Before the election, Herzog said he would do everything he could to spare the country another election cycle, even if that means pressing for a national unity government that brings together rivals Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have previously ruled out partnering with the Arab-led parties .
Former Prime Minister Ehud Barak, however, has said he believes they “can change their mind”, arguing that Netanyahu would do in their position.
“If Netanyahu had a similar problem, he would immediately invite Mansour Abbas”, the leader of Ra’am and “give him the role of a minister of interior”, Barak told France 24 on Friday.
Abbas himself has signalled a willingness to work the opposition camp, saying Eisenkot’s conditions would not pose an obstacle for his party, according to Israel’s Channel 12.
Yousef Jabareen from the Arab-led Joint List has also said that his party is ready for the “ousting of the Netanyahu government”.
“The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a true and equal partnership,” he wrote on X.
Even if Arab-led parties do not formally join the opposition’s coalition, they could prop it up from outside by helping it pass a confidence vote in the Knesset.
Raluca Ganea, co-founder of Israeli civil society group Zazim, told Al Jazeera that a coalition between the opposition bloc and the Arab-led parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel “is the only path forward for Israeli democracy as a whole”.
If Herzog’s first candidate fails to form a government within the 42 days, the Israeli president has the option of asking another Knesset member to try to do so within 28 days. If that candidate also fails, a majority of Knesset members could put forward a third candidate, who would have a final 14 days to try to assemble one.
Even without a coalition commanding at least 61 seats, a candidate could still try to form a minority government by relying on outside support from smaller parties, including Arab-led parties, or negotiate a power-sharing arrangement with alternating prime ministers.
If none of these options succeed and deadlock persists, the Knesset would be formally dissolved, and Israelis would return to the polls for another round of elections.
Those elections would have to be called within 90 days.
Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed.
If the process drags out, that could leave Israel’s longest-serving prime minister in power for months more, even if he ultimately fails to become part of the next governing coalition.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic’s $2T IPO could create millionaires—but it’s asking candidates what they’d do if stock hit zero
articles.title_zh: Anthropic’s $2T IPO could create millionaires—but it’s asking candidates what they’d do if stock hit zero
articles.content_orig:
As Anthropic targets a November IPO at a $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation—potentially eclipsing SpaceX’s record —the blockbuster debut could mint a new class of wealthy tech workers among its more than 2,500 employees.
But that potential multimillion-dollar employee windfall appears to be raising concern among company leaders. Anthropic is reportedly asking job candidates during culture interviews how they would feel if the company someday abandoned its AI ambitions for safety reasons—and that decision caused its stock to fall to zero, according to Axios .
“I was honest and said no, I would not be happy if the stock went to 0,” one candidate, who discussed the interview process on the anonymous workplace site Blind , said. “I would want to align doing the most good and remaining ethical while building a sustaining business.”
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who has an estimated net worth of $13.6 billion, has reportedly expressed concerns about the way the company’s enormous financial incentives could affect its ability to retain employees who are genuinely committed to its mission. Anthropic, a public benefit corporation, has long sought to distinguish itself from competition like OpenAI through a broader focus on AI safety and the “long-term benefit of humanity.”
“At the end of the day, the mission is what we’re all here for,” the company’s values statement reads . “It gives us a shared purpose and allows us to act swiftly together, rather than being pulled in multiple directions by competing goals.”
Anthropic is simultaneously fighting to attract the world’s top AI talent while grappling with what could happen if that talent becomes extraordinarily wealthy in the process.
The company is competing with the likes of Meta , Google , Microsoft , and OpenAI for top researchers and engineers—and resultantly offering compensation packages well into the hundreds of thousands of dollars.
The competition is so fierce that Anthropic acknowledged in its S-1 filing dated Oct. 26 that hiring and retaining qualified employees has become exceptionally difficult, particularly in the San Francisco Bay Area, where the company is headquartered.
“Competition in our industry relating to hiring and retaining employees with appropriate qualifications and on competitive economic terms is exceptionally intense and has escalated significantly in recent periods,” the company said.
Anthropic is currently dangling base salaries of $350,000 to $850,000 for staff software engineering roles, for example . And there’s plenty more work to be done. The company currently has more than 600 open roles , including about 120 in sales, over 60 in AI research & engineering, and 50 in security.
In order to land an offer after such a highly competitive process, some candidates are reportedly spending more than $4,000 on private coaching to help them get hired.
“Spend a few thousand dollars, and now your salary goes up by $200,000—that calculus makes sense,” Aline Lerner, founder of prep company Interviewing.io, told Bloomberg .
The potential wealth creation at Anthropic is part of a much bigger phenomenon unfolding across the AI industry.
Following SpaceX’s $1.77 trillion IPO , thousands of current and former employees—from welders and coders to managers and executives— became millionaires as their company equity soared in value . Roughly 400 current and former SpaceX employees saw their stakes become worth more than $100 million.
As AI valuations continue to soar and employees cash in on equity grants, it is expected that more people will see similar wealth booms. However, Amodei has warned that the economic benefits of AI could become concentrated among a relatively small group of people. As a result, he and Anthropic’s other six cofounders , including his sister, Daniela Amodei , committed to giving away 80% of their wealth .
“The thing to worry about is a level of wealth concentration that will break society,” Dario Amodei wrote in a letter published earlier this year.
Amodei called out fellow tech leaders who have grown increasingly skeptical of philanthropy , arguing that wealthy individuals have a responsibility to help address the inequality that AI could exacerbate.
“Wealthy individuals have an obligation to help solve this problem,” Amodei wrote. “It is sad to me that many wealthy individuals (especially in the tech industry) have recently adopted a cynical and nihilistic attitude that philanthropy is inevitably fraudulent or useless.”

The holiday season is hurtling toward us like a freight train, and there's nothing we can do about it — except maybe allow ourselves some retail therapy at Costco, the store that has it all (and in bulk quantities). The wholesale retailer has lots of great new finds for November, so we're highlighting some highly rated items. This month, you'll find cookware, gourmet chocolates, energy drinks, holiday glassware, snacks, and more.
Something to keep in mind about Costco: The store's online inventory and in-store stock aren't always the same. As such, some of these November finds are only available for purchase online. But don't worry — we included links to each product.
You may also notice that our selection is mostly name-brand products, with just one Kirkland Signature item in the mix. While Costco's store brand is beloved for its quality and affordability, the chain stocks a wide selection of name-brand items to ensure members have lots to choose from. Speaking of impressive Kirkland Signature products, here's how Costco's pumpkin pie compares to the one from Sam's Club in terms of tastiness and overall value (after all, it's never too early to start planning your Thanksgiving menu).
This versatile, induction-compatible cookware is great for braising, searing, roasting, and baking. As one Costco member put it in their review, "This braising pan is high quality and even better than I expected. It's my go to pan already for dinner."
You can buy this Tramontina 4-Quart Enameled Cast Iron Covered Braiser online for $58.99.
This gourmet shortbread set comes with 24 individual boxes, which equals 96 cookies in total. That makes them perfect for random gift giving. "I'm going to give out [these cookies] during the holidays to neighbors etc.," wrote a reviewer on the Costco site.
You can buy Mary Macleod's Shortbread Christmas Tree Box of The Classic Shortbread online for $89.99.
If you love crispy snacks but are burned out on chips and pretzels, rice crackers are the next logical step. Dubbed "Best snack crackers ever" by a Costco reviewer, the shopper described them as "Spicy, salty sweet and crunchy you can't do much better." Each 2-pound bag comes with varieties like Chili Mochi, Sesame Half Moon, Wasabi Crescent, and plenty more.
You can buy these Kirkland Signature Rice Crackers online for $12.49.
If you know any chocolate snobs who hold the European view that Hershey's is gross (thanks to one infamous flavor note), Costco has the perfect gift. "Fresh and delicious," wrote a Costco member of this Hebert Candies assortment. "The chocolate itself is fresh and well made, totally European quality." This 2-pound pack comes with 100 individual pieces in milk, white, and dark chocolate.
You can buy this Hebert Candies Heritage Chocolate Assortment online for $59.99.
This mushroom-infused coffee is a good example of at least one of the food trends that swept through 2026 . Featuring a blend of mushrooms intended to support immune function, reduce stress, and improve concentration, the convenient brew received accolades from Costco reviewers, with one writing, "Portable, delicious and good for you and your brain!"
You can buy 60 servings of Wunderground Craft Instant Coffee Plus Mushroom online for $59.99.
"Very worth the price," wrote a Costco shopper about this cute holiday glassware set. You get four glasses with different seasonally inspired designs. They're also very sturdily made; as another reviewer noted, "The design does not sit on the glass but also feels like a small glass object embossed in the glass."
You can buy this four-piece Pandex Holiday Icon Glasses Set online for $29.99.
According to a review on the Costco website, this holiday-inspired soda is "Really good and taste[s] like a frosted cranberry." Along with seasonal varieties, the soda brand offers lots of regular flavors as well. Here's our ranking of every Poppi flavor from worst to best to whet your whistle.
You can buy an 18-pack of Poppi Soda Cranberry Fizz online for $18.99 (price valid through November 15).
Of all the popular ways to pop popcorn , a stovetop popper offers a one-way ticket to nostalgia town. (Did we mention that it's also among the tastiest methods?) With a 4.4-star member rating as of this writing, this GreenPan popper is currently $12 off its regular price and is compatible with gas, electric, and induction cooktops.
You can buy this GreenPan 5.39 qt. Stainless Steel Popcorn Popper online for $45.99 (price valid through November 22).
Here's the awesome thing about gift bundles like this one from Ethel M Chocolates: There's nothing stopping you from keeping one box for yourself and enjoying rich, decadent flavors like Maple Walnut Satin Crème and Macadamia Salute. "Delish," wrote a Costco reviewer of these gourmet chocolates.
You can buy this Ethel M Chocolates Nuts and Caramels Collection Bundle online for $59.99.
While it doesn't rank among the best-selling energy drinks in the U.S. , Ghost is pretty popular in its own right. In the words of one Costco shopper, "Best energy drinks out there. I don't experience any crash, the flavors are phenomenal, and you can't beat the price!!!" This vibe-licious variety pack includes 18 total beverages and comes in Welch's Grape-Cran, Blue Raspberry, and Strawbango flavors.
You can buy this Ghost Energy Drink Variety Pack online for $32.99.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu’s Bid to Stay in Power Will Test His Political Savvy
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu’s Bid to Stay in Power Will Test His Political Savvy
articles.content_orig:
President Isaac Herzog on Sunday called on Israel's political leaders to accept the election results and demonstrate flexibility in coalition negotiations, warning against political entrenchment that could force the country into another election, ahead of consultations at the President’s Residence set to begin on Wednesday.
“The election results are an established fact – they are the reality. And now is the time to tell all the leaders: Stop climbing trees and position yourselves in front of this reality," Herzog said while speaking at the state memorial ceremony for Israel's first president, Chaim Weizmann.
Herzog made the remarks amid the political deadlock in which the election results showed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanayhu's bloc and the bloc seeking to oust the premier both fall short of the required 61-seat Knesset majority.
Netanyahu’s bloc maintained its lead, securing 53 seats in the next Knesset, while the opposition bloc won 48. Meanwhile, the Arab parties, Ra'am and the Joint List, won a record-breaking total of 19 seats combined.
The Joint List and Ra'am are expected to recommend Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot for prime minister during consultations with President Isaac Herzog, a senior Joint List official told Walla on Sunday.
Talks at the President's Residence will begin Wednesday, when Eisenkot is expected to be the first candidate to receive the mandate from the president, giving him 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension, to form a coalition.
Along with the 48 seats won by the opposition bloc, the Arab parties' 19 recommendations would give Eisenkot 67 in total, prompting Herzog to grant him the mandate.
The Knesset is expected to be sworn in on November 10, regardless of any government or coalition talks.
By law, the president is required to consult the Knesset factions before deciding who receives the task of forming a government.
Herzog said that this week, at the President’s Residence, "we will try to put up ladders to allow the leaders to position themselves in front of this reality in a measured and careful manner."
Herzog said he would receive the official election results on Wednesday from Central Elections Committee chairman and Supreme Court Deputy President Justice Noam Sohlberg.
"Following that, I will begin consultations at the President's Residence. The President's Residence will be wide open to all factions and parties."
The president emphasized the importance of cooperation among party leaders, urging them to demonstrate a willingness to consider different proposals and reach agreements.
"I have already said that I hope the representatives will come with open minds, and I add that they should come with open hearts, to listen and share ideas and find creative solutions to prevent another election ," he said.
On Saturday, Eisenkot laid out four principles for joining his proposed coalition, saying that “any MK” willing to accept them could become a partner in forming the next government.
Eisenkot said he intended to establish the broadest possible Zionist, statesmanlike government, bringing together elected representatives who agree on Israel’s fundamental character, national service obligations, and the need to eliminate Hamas’s military and governing capabilities in the Gaza Strip.
Last week, Democrats party leader Yair Golan called on Wednesday for the opposition to form a coalition with the Arab parties.
Other heads of the opposition parties, Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett (B'Yachad), and Avigdor Liberman (Yisrael Beytenu), had drawn a red line to Arab parties being part of the government, saying they are not viable coalition partners after the October 7 massacre in 2023.
The political deadlock could ultimately lead to another election, although the parties may still reach an agreement through coalition negotiations. Other possible outcomes include a unity government among Netanyahu and members of Eisenkot’s bloc, or the formation of a minority government.
The Arab parties have expressed willingness to cooperate with the oppostion bloc to work toward replacing Netanyahu.
Meanwhile, opposition party leaders have also reportedly agreed that their first move after the new Knesset is sworn in on November 10 would be to oust Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana , a member of Netanyahu's Likud party.
The move would require a majority in a Knesset vote and could be achievable with the support of the Arab parties, bringing the potential backing to 67 seats.
Replacing Ohana would give the opposition bloc greater control over the parliamentary agenda, including votes, legislation, and committee appointments, even if Netanyahu remains in office as head of a caretaker government.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: At 97, China’s first female conductor still performs in public, wowing audiences
articles.content_orig:
Zheng notes that she never intentionally pursued a conducting career, choosing instead to ‘let everything happen naturally’
China’s first female conductor, Zheng Xiaoying, is 97 years old, but she continues to give outstanding performances to audiences.
In August, the nonagenarian conducted the Chinese-language version of the opera Carmen in Xiamen, in southeastern China’s Fujian province, where she lives. Tickets for the performance were like gold dust, and audiences marvelled, as always, at her elegant, expressive conducting.
Zheng has led a remarkable life. Born in Shanghai in 1929, she began studying piano at age six. During her university years, she switched to biology and medicine at the prestigious Peking Union Medical College Hospital. But at 19, she decided to flee to the liberated zone in search of “a new world she had never seen.”

Alibaba’s flagship AI model Qwen will be integrated into Apple Intelligence, after years of speculation and regulatory uncertainty
Apple’s long-awaited artificial intelligence features will be officially launched in China in December, ending two years of regulatory uncertainty as the US tech giant seeks to bring advanced technologies to its second-largest market with the help of Alibaba Group Holding.
The first batch of Apple Intelligence services will roll out to Chinese iPhone users alongside the iOS 27.3 update in December, following an open beta test with developers starting November 4, the US company said in a statement on Saturday.
The initial roll-out will include around 18 new features provided by Apple Intelligence, including writing tools for summarising and proofreading, live translation for phone calls and messages, as well as visual intelligence via camera controls, according to the statement.

articles.title_orig: Rioters smash, loot storefronts amid cost of living protests in Germany
articles.title_zh: Rioters smash, loot storefronts amid cost of living protests in Germany
articles.content_orig:
Masked rioters smashed storefronts and looted goods late Saturday in Frankfurt, Germany amid a protest against the rising cost of living.
The largely peaceful demonstrations were led by a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" - roughly translated to "Gen Z's got this" - rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.
Tensions peaked in the evening as some groups of protesters refused to disperse, sparking clashes and violence in major cities including Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg.
in Frankfurt's financial hub, masked protesters hurled stones, fireworks and pepper bombs, according to police.
Authorities also said looters stole weapons from a gun store, which were later retrieved. Some rioters also threw Molotov cocktails at police after pummeling them with stones and bottles earlier in the day, Frankfurt police said on X.
In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police responded by using water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds.
Earlier in the day, demonstrations had been largely peaceful. In Berlin, young protesters gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.
"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection - in short, in our future - because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.
Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.
"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.
AFP contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Military briefing: what would another US-Iran conflict look like?
articles.title_zh: Military briefing: what would another US-Iran conflict look like?
articles.content_orig:
Israel could unleash a devastating surprise attack targeting Iran's top military leaders if war resumes after Tuesday's midterm elections, potentially employing tactics similar to its sophisticated 2024 operation that crippled Hezbollah, the New York Post reported Saturday.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier is reportedly heading to the Middle East to join the USS George Washington and USS George W. Bush as President Donald Trump weighs renewed military action against Tehran.
Trump told Kansas City radio station KCMO Friday that the conflict is "going to get wrapped up soon," although he did not elaborate.
Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., predicted military action could come immediately after the elections.
"I'm going to guess about a day or three after this election, I would not want to be anywhere close to Iran," Marshall said Thursday.
Former Mossad Deputy Head of Global Operations Oded Ailam told the outlet that Israel could execute another operation resembling its extraordinary September 2024 pager attack against Hezbollah, this time targeting four Iranian military hard-liners believed to exercise effective control over the regime.
"This is the bread and butter of Israeli strategy, is surprise twists and turns, unexpected moves and I'm absolutely certain that Israel has cards in the sleeve that will be used," Ailam said.
The 2024 operation was among the most creative, planned and devastating intelligence attacks in modern warfare.
On Sept. 17-18, thousands of explosive-rigged pagers and walkie-talkies used by Hezbollah operatives detonated across Lebanon and Syria, killing dozens, injuring thousands and severely disrupting the Iranian-backed terrorist organization's communications.
The meticulously coordinated attack required years of planning, sophisticated intelligence gathering, and infiltration of Hezbollah's communications supply chain, demonstrating Israel's extraordinary ability to identify, penetrate, and strike its enemies from within.
That precedent raises the possibility that Israeli intelligence already knows the identities, movements, and vulnerabilities of Iran's military leadership and has spent years preparing similarly unexpected operations.
According to Ailam, Iran's real power rests with four military figures: Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander Ahmad Vahidi, Basij commander Hossein Taeb, armed forces chief Ali Abdollahi and Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei.
"The president and foreign minister can't make decisions. [The military junta] hides behind Mojtaba, but he's not in charge; he's a complete puppet," Ailam said, referring to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.
"Israel will use its imagination, its intelligence and the ability of the Israelis to surprise and turn the table in ways you can not anticipate," he added.
Ailam said the Iranian leadership is increasingly divided over negotiations with Washington, with military hard-liners repeatedly undermining diplomatic efforts.
"They're not on the same page themselves, we see a lot of friction within the regime, different approaches, agreeing then reneging," he said.
Retired U.S. Gen. Jack Keane advocated strikes against Iran's leadership, nuclear facilities, energy infrastructure and missile and drone production capabilities.
"The intelligence we have now as a result of six months of collection during the on-again, off-again ceasefire is significant," Keane said.
Ailam suggested that another Israeli intelligence operation could inflict psychological damage exceeding that of a conventional military invasion.
"The effect is enormous, especially on the psychology of the enemy. Imagine after the attack there's a conversation somewhere in a bunker with the top echelons of Iran and everybody's looking to the left and to the right and thinking the guy next to him is a spy," he said.
However, analysts warned that renewed attacks could provoke devastating Iranian retaliation.
"[The regime's] interest is survival; they'll fight harder," said Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
Former IDF Maj. Gen. Yaakov Amidror warned that Iranian strikes against Gulf energy infrastructure could trigger an overwhelming Israeli response.
"If the Iranian retaliation will be to destroy or try to destroy energy facilities in the Gulf countries, that would be a good excuse for Israel to destroy the whole energy infrastructure in Iran," Amidror said.
"This is something that cannot be rebuilt in a few years, this will send Iran back 50 years," he added.
Meanwhile, Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., pushed back against the Trump administration's reported military planning.
"Their plan is insane. It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law," Murphy said Thursday.
"The plan that they have developed will lead in my view to a prolongment and an escalation of this war that in my view will be devastating for our security interests," he added.
Despite any speculation about a leadership strike, Amidror emphasized that Israel's overriding military priority remains eliminating Iran's nuclear weapons potential and ballistic missile capabilities.

articles.title_orig: Reeves says UK's future should be inside the EU
articles.title_zh: Reeves says UK's future should be inside the EU
articles.content_orig:
Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves has argued the UK's future should be inside the EU, and that Brexit has made the country "poorer, weaker and less secure".
In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury, Reeves said she welcomed debate around the UK's relationship with Europe.
At the last election, Labour's manifesto said a Labour government would stay outside the EU and make Brexit work.
But Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there needs to be an honest discussion about what the future relationship looks like.
The Conservatives have said there is no desire to rerun the Brexit debate and Reform UK's Nigel Farage has said there is no mandate to pursue closer EU ties.
Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
Burnham has said that any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is next due by 2029.
In the Sunday Times , Reeves wrote: "No-one in the Treasury ever doubted where my instincts were. I do believe Britain's future lies in the European Union."
She said supporters of rejoining the EU had to "make the argument, demonstrate tangible benefits and to get the next steps right".
Reeves added that at the forthcoming UK-EU summit, she hoped for confirmation of the youth mobility scheme she has been pushing for since she was in office.
She also said she was hoping for "progress towards entry" into the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) scheme.
Announced last March, SAFE is part of an EU-wide effort to rearm after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A defence pact agreed with the EU last May paved the way for UK-based defence companies to be part of projects funded by SAFE.
In her piece for the Sunday Times, Reeves also sought to defend her record in office.
She wrote about the need for governments to be "braver" in building big infrastructure projects and "clear eyed" about the risks and benefits AI would drive in advanced economies.

articles.content_orig:
Thousands of people have rallied in Tel Aviv to urge the Israeli opposition to make a deal with Arab parties to remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Protesters at Saturday’s rally told the AFP news agency this may be the “last chance for real change” and that Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, is a “great manipulator”.
Main opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has previously ruled out forming a coalition with Israel’s Arab parties, but a deadlock in Tuesday’s elections means siding with the parties could help him form a government.
“People really want this vote for change to work out, and they believe that… Gadi Eisenkot and other leaders of the Jewish-Israeli parties need to listen to their voice,” Al Jazeera correspondent Nour Odeh said from Ramallah on Saturday.
Counter-protesters also showed up to Saturday’s demonstrations, with Netanyahu supporters seen shouting their own demands that “Israel should not have a government with so-called terrorists”, Odeh said.
Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday’s elections, while Eisenkot’s won 48, meaning neither side can form a government in Israel’s 120-seat parliament alone.
Israel’s three Arab-led parties won 19 seats, having made significant gains in Tuesday’s election.
Nearly 840,000 people voted for Ra’am and the Joint List, a coalition of three Arab-led parties, a 64 percent increase from the last elections in 2022, according to the Central Election Committee.
The Arab electoral success means a coalition with Eisenkot would provide a comfortable majority of 67. However, for many in Israel, the idea of siding with Arabs is politically unpalatable.
Netanyahu has accused Palestinian-Israeli parties of “stealing” the polls and accepting funding from Qatar to do it. Qatar has rejected the allegations , calling it a disinformation campaign.
Odeh said that Israeli right-wing circles have described “the historic turnout of Palestinian Israelis as electoral terrorism, equating it to the October 7th attack”, when Hamas-led fighters stormed southern Israel, killing more than 1,200 people and taking hundreds captive.
“Palestinian-Israeli votes and voices” are under attack because they have a “prominent position” in deciding whether Eisenkot can form a government, she added.
